title: The Roads Between
text: The question this section was meant to answer is where pumas are killed by vehicles. That question cannot be answered here yet, because the data that would answer it are not in hand. So this section does two things instead: it states plainly what is missing, and it presents the best interim proxy the analysis can support — where the corridor and dangerous roads coincide — without dressing that proxy up as a mortality count.

title: The Roads Between
text:
What is missing, and why
Direct roadkill records for the Bay Area are held in the California Roadkill Observation System (CROS), maintained by the UC Davis Road Ecology Center. A data request is with F. Shilling there; at the time of writing, no reply has been received (Decision 11). The project does not scrape or reconstruct those records — they are used with authorisation or not at all. Until they arrive, there is no published mortality-point layer in this project, and none is fabricated to fill the gap. When the CROS records are available, they will overlay the risk surface below as a validation layer — confirming or correcting where the proxy points.
That is the honest state of Question 4: the mortality map is pending, not withheld.

title: The Roads Between
section: The interim proxy — where traffic meets the corridor
text:
The interim proxy — where traffic meets the corridor
What the analysis can say comes from combining two things it already knows: how busy each road is (traffic volume, from the crossing analysis in the connectivity section) and whether that road sits inside the core corridor, where a puma is most likely to actually move. Collision risk is highest where both are true — a busy road and the core corridor in the same place.
This is a sharper filter than traffic alone. The connectivity section ranked road crossings by traffic, and several busy roads appeared near the top. But most of those busy roads clip the corridor at its permeable edges, not through its core. When the core-corridor filter is applied, the risk picture narrows sharply.








Figure 1: Collision-risk proxy: road crossings where traffic and the core corridor coincide. Crossings inside the core corridor are coloured by traffic volume (amber to red); crossings outside the core are greyed — they are barriers, but not where a puma is most likely to cross. US-101 at Coyote Valley is the one crossing that is both high-traffic and inside the core corridor, which makes it the clear top collision risk. This is a proxy from road traffic and corridor overlap, not a mortality count; direct roadkill records (CROS) are pending. No puma locations are shown. Source: corridor × road crossings (Decisions 33–34).




The map makes the filter visible. Most of the busy roads the corridor crosses turn grey, because they clip the corridor outside its core. What stays coloured — busy and in the core — is dominated by one road: US-101 at Coyote Valley. It is the single crossing that is both high-traffic and inside the core corridor, and so it is the clear top collision-risk location, not merely the top barrier.

title: The Roads Between
text:
The risk ranking
Ranking the crossings by the two factors together — traffic volume and core-corridor membership — puts US-101 alone at the top. The next-busiest roads fall away because they sit outside the core; the other in-core roads are quiet.

Top road crossings by traffic and core-corridor overlap. Only US-101 is both high-traffic and in-core — the combination that defines collision risk. Traffic values are directly measured; see the connectivity section for the full confidence-tiered ranking.

The reading is straightforward and narrow, which is the honest result: one road carries most of the corridor’s collision risk. Santa Cruz Highway and Route 17 are busy, but the corridor crosses them at its edges, not its core. Big Basin Way and Summit Road are in the core, but they are quiet mountain roads. US-101 is the only place where heavy traffic and the core corridor meet — which is exactly why it is both the top barrier and the top mitigation priority.

title: The Roads Between
text:
What would change this
This proxy stands in for mortality data, and it should be replaced by mortality data when that becomes available. The CROS records, once authorised, would show where vehicle strikes have actually happened — which may confirm the US-101 finding, or reveal risk on roads the proxy underweights. Two honest limits apply until then: the proxy assumes risk scales with traffic and corridor overlap, which is reasonable but untested here; and the corridor itself is a landscape-cost model, not observed movement, so both inputs to the risk picture are hypotheses. The proxy points to where to look first. It does not close the question.

title: Room to Move
text: The puma question is the opposite of the bobcat one. There are too few puma records to model where the animals are, and the precise locations that do exist are sensitive enough that publishing them would do harm. So this section does not map where pumas were seen. It maps where the landscape would let one move — built from the shape of the land, not from sightings.

title: Room to Move
text:
Built from resistance, not sightings
Every layer in this section rests on a resistance surface: a map of how costly each 1 km cell is for a puma to cross, high where the land is developed, steep, or busy with roads, low where it is protected open ground. The surface is assembled from land cover, terrain, human modification, and traffic — not from where anyone recorded a puma.
That has one consequence worth stating up front, because it is the mirror image of the bobcat result. The bobcat occupancy model had to correct for recording effort, because it was built from sightings. The puma corridors carry no effort term at all — there are no sightings in them to be biased. Where the puma corridors agree with a density surface, they agree for a structural reason, not because both were shaped by the same observers. This is the clean half of Question 5.

title: Room to Move
section: Why you see a band, not a line
text:
Why you see a band, not a line
The core result is a corridor between the two largest habitat blocks in the region: the Santa Cruz Mountains and the southern Diablo Range, linked across the south Bay through the Coyote Valley pinch where US-101 cuts the gap. The least-cost path between them runs 37.2 km and passes within 1.6 km of the verified Coyote Valley crossing.
But the maps below lead with a band, not that line, and the reason is a real limit, not a stylistic choice. A least-cost path is a single-cell-wide thread through a 1 km grid. It looks precise, and that precision is false: move the input weights a little and the thread shifts by a kilometre or more. The honest product is the swath — the zone of low-cost cells around the path — shown in two tiers:

a core band (the lowest-cost 2% of corridor cells, 409 km²) — high-confidence corridor,
a context band (the lowest-cost 5%, 1,021 km²) — the permeable flanks around it.

The swath says what the analysis can actually support: the corridor runs through here, in this zone, not the corridor is this exact line. The precise pinch at Coyote Valley is located separately, by road geometry in the crossing analysis below — not by the swath, whose 1 km grain is too coarse to resolve a sub-kilometre constriction.








Figure 1: The Santa Cruz Mountains ↔︎ southern Diablo Range puma corridor, shown as a two-tier swath over the protected core habitat it connects. The darker core band is the lowest-cost 2% of corridor cells (409 km²), a high-confidence corridor; the lighter context band is the lowest-cost 5% (1,021 km²), the permeable flanks around it. Faint green blocks are the 164 core habitat patches; the two bold-outlined blocks are the corridor endpoints — Santa Cruz Mountains and the southern Diablo Range. The corridor runs through this zone, not along a single line — the band is the honest product at a 1 km grain. The precise US-101 pinch at Coyote Valley is located by road geometry in the crossing map below, not by this swath. No puma locations are shown; this is generalised corridor geometry. Source: least-cost corridor (Decision 33) over core patches (Decision 32).

title: Room to Move
section: Where the corridor meets the roads
text:
Where the corridor meets the roads
A corridor is only as good as its worst crossing. Where the swath meets a major road, the road is a barrier whose severity scales with traffic, not just with presence — a quiet two-lane road and a freeway are not the same obstacle. So each crossing is ranked by traffic volume.
The top barrier is US-101 at Coyote Valley, at 142,000 vehicles a day. Getting that number right took a correction. An earlier version of the analysis, using a spatial traffic-data join, dropped US-101 here to a modelled floor of about 80,000 — a 43% underestimate — and let a lower-traffic arterial outrank it. The fix referenced the traffic data along the highway route by postmile, recovered the real 142k, and re-ran the corridor (Decision 34). US-101 is now correctly the top-ranked crossing.
One honest detail in that ranking: crossings are ranked within traffic-data confidence tiers, not on the raw number alone. A road whose volume is measured directly outranks one whose volume is filled in by name-matching, even when the filled-in number is close. This stops a lower-confidence estimate from masquerading as the top barrier — the exact failure the US-101 correction fixed.








Figure 2: Where the puma corridor crosses roads, ranked by traffic, zoomed to the crossing zone in the south Bay. All 290 crossing segments are shown on a neutral road basemap so each sits on its road; line thickness scales with traffic volume (AADT) and solid lines are directly-measured volumes while dashed lines are estimated (modelled, name-filled, or spatially filled — read these as lower-confidence). The four named roads the corridor crosses are outlined and labelled; US-101 at Coyote Valley, at 142,000 vehicles a day, is the top barrier by a wide margin. Unnamed high-traffic links (freeway ramps) appear as thick base-layer lines but are not promoted to named barriers, since one class label covers many separate crossings. No puma locations are shown. Source: corridor × road crossings, AADT by Decision 34.

title: Room to Move
section: The network, and a distinction that matters
text:
The network, and a distinction that matters
Widening from the single corridor to the whole system of large habitat blocks — the 29 cores of at least 30 km² — gives a connectivity network: each core linked to its geometric neighbours, each link routed through the resistance surface. Two findings come out of it, and holding them apart is the point.
Coyote Valley is the efficient link, and the traffic barrier — but not the structural weak point. The cheapest connections in the network — the strongest links — run through the south Bay, between the cores on either side of the Coyote Valley gap. That is where the two halves of the region connect at low cost. Those south-Bay links are the efficient path; the cross-bay alternatives cost far more. So Coyote Valley matters twice — as the real, protectable connection, and as the 142k traffic barrier astride it — but it is a strong link, not a weak one.
The structural weak links are the cross-bay spans. The costliest connections in the network are the long, high-resistance routes that would join the Peninsula / Santa Cruz cluster to the East-Bay / Diablo cluster across the central urbanized Bay — spans of 40 to 60 km with no stepping stones between them. The central Bay effectively splits the system into two subnetworks, joined efficiently only at the south end, through Coyote Valley. This matches what is already known: Santa Cruz Mountains pumas are famously isolated, connected to the Diablo Range mainly via the south Bay.
The traffic pinch and the structural weak point are therefore two different things on two different axes. Coyote Valley is a traffic-mitigation priority — a real corridor with a dangerous road across it. The cross-bay gaps are a fragmentation finding — evidence of what is already disconnected.
And the cross-bay links are not corridors to build. This distinction matters enough to state plainly: a 60 km least-cost path across the developed bayshore is at the edge of biological plausibility. The network method forces a route between geometric neighbours whether or not a real one exists, and the routing dutifully finds the least-bad line across an essentially impassable barrier. Those longest cross-bay links mean these clusters are effectively disconnected, not here is a corridor to protect. Read them as fragmentation evidence. The south-Bay connection, by contrast, is a real connection worth protecting.








Figure 3: The puma core-connectivity network over the core habitat it links. Faint green blocks are the core habitat patches. Links between cores are drawn as schematic lines coloured by cost — green links are cheap and strong (the efficient south-Bay connections), red links are costly and weak. The lines show connectivity topology, not exact routes: at a 1 km grain a single-cell path would imply false precision, so the lines say which cores connect and how cheaply, not where a puma walks. The three-to-five costliest links — the structural weak points — are shown instead as red swaths, the honest band form, because those fragile cross-bay connections are the map’s real subject. Read the red cross-bay swaths as evidence of disconnection, not as corridors to protect: the method forces a route between geometric neighbours whether or not a real one exists, and a 40–60 km path across the developed bayshore is at the edge of plausibility. No puma locations are shown. Source: Gabriel-graph network (Decision 37, corrected by Decision 38).

title: Room to Move
section: What this section is, and is not
text:
What this section is, and is not
These corridors are hypotheses about movement drawn from a landscape-cost model, not tracks from collared animals. No puma was followed to draw them; there is no telemetry here to confirm them. Shifting the model’s weights within a plausible range moves the corridor by up to about 1.5 km, so the routes are stable in location but not exact to the metre. They are the best structural estimate of where connectivity runs — a well-founded hypothesis, and the right basis for asking where to look and where to protect, but a hypothesis.
Every puma layer here is shown as generalised geometry — bands and routes, never points. That is deliberate and required: precise puma locations are a poaching and disturbance risk, so the project never publishes them. Nothing in this section is fine enough to reverse-engineer a den, a kill site, or a camera. The corridors are about where an animal could move, at the scale of the landscape, not about where any individual animal is.

title: The Protected-Land Fabric
text: The first question is about the ground itself, before any animal moves across it. How much protected open space is there in the ten-county Bay Area, how is it held, and how does it break apart when you look at it the way a wide-ranging carnivore would — as a set of patches large enough to hold a home range, or not?

title: The Protected-Land Fabric
text:
Two kinds of protection
Protected land here comes in two forms, and the difference matters for a puma. Fee land is owned outright for conservation: the parks, watershed lands, and open-space preserves that most people picture. Easement land is private ground — often working ranchland — where the owner has sold or donated the right to develop it, so it stays open. To a puma crossing it, an easement grazing parcel next to a fee preserve is one continuous piece of habitat. Tenure is a legal distinction, not an ecological one.
The project keeps both. The connectivity track uses a union of the two sources: CPAD fee land and CCED conservation easements, merged into one protected-land layer, with fee taking precedence wherever the two map the same ground so no area is counted twice.

title: The Protected-Land Fabric
section: How much, and how much is new
text:
How much, and how much is new
The union holds 5,996.5 km² of protected land across the ten counties. Fee land accounts for 4,720.8 km² of that, spread over 1,129 CPAD units. The easements add 1,275.7 km² of genuinely new protected ground — a roughly 27% increase over the fee footprint alone — after removing 498.2 km² where easements overlapped land already protected in fee.
That 27% is the point worth holding on to. Conservation easements are not a rounding error on the map of Bay Area protected land. More than a quarter of the connectivity fabric — much of it working ranchland along the inner Coast Ranges — exists only because of easements. Leave them out and the protected-land picture looks substantially more fragmented than it is.
One limit on this comes with the easement data. Where the easement layer has no record, that does not mean the land is unprotected — only that no easement is mapped there. The union labels tenure where the data exists; it does not fill gaps. Read the easement totals as a floor, not a full accounting.

title: The Protected-Land Fabric
section: From protected land to habitat patches
text:
From protected land to habitat patches
A wide-ranging carnivore does not experience protected land as a legal inventory. It experiences it as patches — connected pieces of open ground it can settle in or move through. So the next step dissolves the union: fee and easement melt together wherever they touch, and the result is cut into distinct patches by physical contiguity, not by ownership.
Most of those patches are small. The patch-area distribution is a smooth size continuum, from thousands of tiny fragments up to a handful of very large blocks, with no natural break to cut on. A break would let the data choose the threshold; there isn’t one, so the threshold comes from the animal instead.
A puma home range spans tens to hundreds of square kilometres. A protected patch smaller than about 5 km² cannot hold a meaningful fraction of even one such range, so it works as a stepping-stone at most, not as a place a resident animal lives. Setting that 5 km² floor — an ecological scale, not a number read off a curve — leaves 164 core patches large enough to anchor a home range. The floor still retains 82.5% of all protected area, because the area that gets dropped sits in thousands of tiny fragments that together hold very little ground.








Figure 1: Patch count against the minimum-area floor. Each candidate floor is plotted with the number of patches that survive it; the amber point marks the chosen 5 km² floor, which keeps 164 patches and 82.5% of all protected area. The curve is a smooth continuum with no natural break, so the floor is set by the puma home-range scale rather than by a gap in the data. Source: Decision 32 floor scan (tbl_17).





This is the floor scan, not the raw size distribution: it shows how many patches survive each candidate threshold, and it is the evidence that the 5 km² cut is not severe. Most of what the floor removes is thousands of tiny fragments; the protected area they hold barely moves the total.
This is the structural shape of the problem. Of nearly 4,000 protected patches, only 164 are large enough to anchor a wide-ranging carnivore, and the habitat value concentrates in a small number of very large cores — the Santa Cruz Mountains block at 177 km², the southern Diablo Range at 500 km², and a short list of others. The rest of the protected fabric is stepping-stones and fragments between them.

title: The Protected-Land Fabric
section: What this section does and does not claim
text:
What this section does and does not claim
This is a description of the protected land, built from protected-area boundaries alone. It uses no occurrence records, so the detection-effort caveat that governs the occurrence maps later in this project does not apply here — there is nothing in these numbers that reflects where people looked for animals. The patches are where the protected ground is, not where the cats were seen.
What it does not tell you is whether an animal can actually move between those 164 cores. A patch being large is not the same as a patch being reachable. Two cores can sit a few kilometres apart on the map and be effectively cut off from each other by a freeway, a reservoir, or the developed bayshore. Turning this static fabric into a question about movement — which cores connect, and where the connections are weakest — is the work of the puma connectivity section (Question 3).

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
This page explains the four main methods behind the maps on this site, for a reader who is not a spatial analyst. Each one gets a plain definition, a worked example, and a note on what it can and cannot tell you. The full processing log, every parameter value, and the numbered decisions live in docs/methodology.md.
One idea runs through all four, and it is worth stating once at the top: a record is not the animal. Every method here starts from points that people reported — where a puma or a bobcat was seen or photographed. People do not look everywhere equally. So each method is, in part, a way to deal with that unevenness. Two of the methods below describe the records; one tries to remove the effort from them; one does not use the records at all. Keeping track of which is which is the whole point of the Effort page.

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
Kernel density (KDE)
What it is. Kernel density turns a scatter of points into a smooth surface. At every place on the map it asks: how many records are near here, and how near? Close records count for more than far ones. The result is a heat surface — warm where records cluster, cool where they are sparse.






Figure 1: A worked kernel-density surface. The green circles are the raw point records. The grey bands are the density surface built from them — darker where points are dense, fading outward. Two dense cores are joined by a lower-density bridge, with a small outlying blob below. The bandwidth sets how far each point’s influence spreads, and so how much the cores merge or stay separate.



Illustration from Spatial Analysis Online (de Smith, Goodchild & Longley), used to show the method. It is not Bay Area cat data.
The one setting that matters: bandwidth. Bandwidth is the width of the smoothing. A narrow bandwidth hugs each point tightly and gives a spiky surface; a wide bandwidth blurs the points together into broad zones. The choice changes the map, so it must be made on a rule, not by eye.






TipWorked example — the two cats used different bandwidths, on purpose



For bobcat, an automatic selector (bw.ppl) passed the pre-set rule and chose a bandwidth of about 1,110 m. Bobcat records are dense, so a tight smoothing still gives a stable surface.
For puma, the same automatic selectors failed the rule — they returned values so small (as low as 49 m) that the surface would have been a scatter of pinpricks, not a density. So the bandwidth was set from biology instead: about 5,000 m, roughly a puma home-range scale. This is why the puma density map shows broad warm regions, not sharp spots.


What it can and cannot tell you. KDE shows where records concentrate. It does not show where animals are, because the records are effort-shaped — warm can mean “many pumas” or “many observers.” On this site the KDE surfaces are always read with that caveat, and the puma KDE is used only as a cross-check, never as a distribution result.

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
Hot spots (Getis-Ord Gi*)
What it is. A hot-spot statistic asks a sharper question than KDE: is the clustering here more than you would expect by chance? For each open-space unit, Gi* compares that unit and its neighbours against the whole study area. A unit with a high count, surrounded by other high-count units, becomes a statistically significant hot spot. The reverse — low counts among low counts — is a cold spot.
“Neighbours” has to be defined. A unit’s Gi* score depends on which units count as its neighbours. Here, neighbours are units within a set distance (about 6,342 m), with a floor so that even a remote unit still has some neighbours to compare against.
Why the correction matters. Testing over a thousand units at once means some will look “significant” by pure luck. A false-discovery-rate correction (Benjamini-Hochberg) tightens the bar so the surviving hot spots are ones you can trust are real clustering, not chance.






Figure 2: The Getis-Ord Gi* flow, panel by panel. Input data — a value per unit (here median income, a generic example). Z-scores — each unit scored on how far its neighbourhood sum sits from the study-area average; strong positive (brown) and strong negative (purple) stand out. P-values — how likely each score is by chance. Hot spots — the final map, keeping only units that pass the significance bar: red are hot (high-value clusters), blue are cold (low-value clusters), pale is not significant.



Illustration from the UCGIS GIS&T Body of Knowledge (Hot Spots and Getis-Ord Gi* Analysis). The example maps income, not wildlife — the method is the same; on this site the value is the puma or bobcat record count.






TipWorked example — the effort check on top



A record hot spot has two possible causes: real animals, or hard surveying. So each hot spot is cross-read against a map of survey effort. If a unit is a record hot spot and an effort hot spot, it is flagged suspect — it may just be where people looked. If it is a record hot spot but not an effort hot spot, it is trusted. On the Effort page you can see this split drawn directly: solid units are trusted, dashed units are suspect.


What it can and cannot tell you. Gi* tells you where clustering is stronger than chance, and — with the effort check — how much of that is likely real. It still rests on the same effort-shaped records, so the effort flag is part of the result, not a footnote.

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
Occupancy modelling
What it is. Occupancy modelling is the one method here that tries to remove the effort problem instead of just flagging it. It splits the question into two parts and fits them in order:

Detection. Given that a bobcat is present in a unit, how likely was it to be recorded, given how much people surveyed there? This is fitted first, with presence held constant, so the model learns the shape of the effort signal.
Occupancy. With the detection part fixed, the model then estimates the probability the animal is actually present, corrected for that effort.

The output is a presence surface that has the survey effort taken out — which is why it can, and does, disagree with the raw record density.
The two parts are two linked equations. For a unit \(i\) and a visit \(j\):
\[
\underbrace{z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_i)}_{\text{occupancy: is the unit occupied?}}
\qquad
\underbrace{y_{ij} \mid z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_i \, p_{ij})}_{\text{detection: was the animal recorded, if present?}}
\]

\(\psi_i\) is the probability the unit is occupied — what we want.
\(p_{ij}\) is the probability of recording the animal on a visit, given it is present. This is where survey effort enters.
\(z_i\) is the true (hidden) presence, 0 or 1. The term \(z_i\,p_{ij}\) encodes the key rule: you can only detect what is there — if \(z_i = 0\), no record is possible, and a non-record where \(z_i = 1\) is a missed detection, not an absence.

Each side is modelled on covariates through a logit link — occupancy on habitat (\(\text{logit}(\psi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i}\)) and detection on effort (\(\text{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \, \text{effort}_{ij}\)). Fitting the detection side first is what lets the model tell “the animal was absent” apart from “nobody looked.”






TipWorked example — bobcat



The bobcat detection part was fitted first. A term for recording effort (the number of prior records in a unit) beat a no-effort model by a wide margin (about 408 AICc units — a very strong preference), confirming effort really does shape the raw records. With that fixed, the presence model was fitted over 845 open-space units. The result is the ψ (psi) surface on the Bobcat page — and it barely correlates with the raw density map (r = 0.075), because the model pulled the effort signal out. That disagreement is the method working, not failing.


Why puma does not get this. Occupancy modelling needs enough repeat records per unit to separate detection from presence. Puma records are too few and too obscured for a defensible fit, so the puma track uses connectivity (below) instead. This was a planned fork, not a shortfall.
What it can and cannot tell you. Occupancy gives the cleanest presence estimate on the site, but only for bobcat, and only where enough units had repeat surveys — 284 units could not be modelled and are drawn as a distinct grey, never as “low occupancy.”

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
Cost-corridor (puma connectivity)
What it is. The puma corridor is built from the landscape, not from records. It answers a movement question: if a puma travels between two large habitat cores, which route costs it the least? “Cost” here means difficulty of movement — open built-up land and busy roads are expensive to cross; forest and shrub are cheap.
It is a three-step chain, and the map below shows all three.

Resistance surface (the input). Every 1 km cell is scored 1–100 for how hard it is to move through. The score is a weighted blend: 45% human modification, 40% land cover, 15% slope, with busy roads overriding the blend where they cross. 1 is freely permeable (good forest); 100 is a wall (dense city, a major freeway).
Cost-corridor surface (the output). From the resistance surface, the model accumulates the total cost of routing between the two cores, in both directions. Low values trace the preferential route; high values are off-route.






NoteWhat ‘least-cost’ actually means



Think of the resistance surface as terrain where every 1 km step has a price — cheap through forest, dear across a freeway. The least-cost path is the route between the two cores whose total price is lowest, the same idea as a sat-nav finding the shortest drive, except the “distance” is movement difficulty, not kilometres.
The algorithm works outward from a core, giving every cell its cumulative cost — the cheapest running total to reach it from the core. Do this from both cores and add the two surfaces, and each cell then holds the cost of the best route through it from core to core. That summed surface is the cost-corridor. The single cheapest line through it is the least-cost path; the low-cost slice around that line is the swath. A swath is used, not the bare line, because the exact line is a fragile artifact — shift one weight slightly and it hops a cell — while the slice is stable and honest about that uncertainty.


The swath (the published product). The swath is simply the lowest-cost slice of the cost-corridor surface — the cheapest ~5% of cells to move through (a narrower core ~2% inside it). That slice, drawn as a band, is the corridor you see on the Puma page.







NoteWhy the corridor uses no records



Because resistance is built only from land cover, human modification, slope, and traffic, the corridor never “sees” where pumas were reported. That is deliberate: it means when the corridor lands on the observed record density (the Effort page convergence finding), the agreement was not built in — it is evidence the pattern is real, not an effort shadow.


The map below shows the chain. The resistance surface (the input) underneath, the cheapest-route cost-corridor over it, and the two-tier swath outline on top — so you can read “the swath is the lowest-cost slice of this surface” directly.








Figure 3: The puma connectivity method, in three layers. Base: the movement-resistance surface (1 = freely permeable, 100 = near-impassable), built from human modification, land cover, slope, and major roads — no records used. Middle: the cost-corridor surface, the accumulated least-cost of routing between the two habitat cores. Top: the two-tier swath outline — the lowest-cost slice of that surface (core ≤ q2%, context ≤ q5%), which is the corridor published on the Puma page. Both rasters are published at the 1 km grain the sensitive-data policy requires. This is a method illustration, not a result.




You can toggle the three layers with the control at top-right — turn the resistance base off to see the cheapest-route cost-corridor alone, or turn everything off but the swath to see the published corridor. The point of stacking them is to make the chain legible: the corridor is not drawn by hand, and it is not drawn from sightings; it falls out of the landscape, one step at a time.






ImportantA method illustration, not a result



This map is here to explain how the corridor is built. The corridor result — where it runs, where it crosses roads, and how it reads against the record density — is on the Puma and Effort pages. The exact route has some play in it (about 1.5 km, tied to the human-modification weight); the two-tier swath, not the centre-line, is the honest product.

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
Where the detail lives
Every choice on this page — the bandwidth rule, the neighbour distance, the model sets, the resistance weights and their sources, and the sensitivity checks that tested them — is recorded as a numbered decision in docs/methodology.md, with the data sources in docs/data-sources.md and the layer schemas in docs/data-dictionary.md.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text: Two species share the same ground here, and they present opposite problems. Bobcats are common and easy to record. Pumas are rare, wide-ranging, and their precise locations are a risk to publish. One landscape, two data situations that point in different directions. This project keeps them on separate tracks and lets each tell its own story.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text:
Not a recovery story
The sister project to this one studied tiger recovery in India. That study had a national census: five repeated survey rounds that made “population change over time” the natural question to ask.
The Bay Area has no equivalent for either species. There is one recent statewide mountain lion abundance estimate and no statewide bobcat estimate at all. A recovery narrative is not available, because the census that would support it does not exist.
What the region does have is dense, well-kept open data on land protection, road mortality, and landscape structure. So the question changes. This project is about distribution and coexistence at the urban–wildland edge — where the animals are, how they move, and where their movement meets the roads — not about recovery over time.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text:
Ten counties, eight million people
The study area is the ten-county San Francisco Bay Area: Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, Solano, and Sonoma. Roughly eight million people live inside this frame, next to a patchwork of parks, watershed lands, ranch easements, and open-space preserves.
Pumas and bobcats persist here at the urban edge, not in wilderness. That edge is the subject. The relevant questions are about movement, permeability, and coexistence, not about a return to some earlier state.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text:
Two species, two tracks
The two species are analysed in parallel and never pooled. This is a fixed rule of the project (Decision 3), and it follows directly from their data. Pooling sparse, sensitive puma records with abundant, low-risk bobcat records would hide the very contrast that makes each track work.









Puma
Bobcat

Sparse
Abundant


Location sensitivity

Low


Home range
Very large (100s of km²)
Small (10s of km²)


Primary story

Occupancy and distribution


Primary method
Least-cost paths and corridors
Occupancy models, KDE, Gi*



The puma track holds 1,028 precise, publicly shared occurrence points inside the study frame. That number is small for an animal that ranges over hundreds of square kilometres, so the puma work is built around connectivity: where the core habitat patches are, and how an animal could move between them. The precise points are never published — every puma map is generalised first. How that is done is set out in the sensitive-data policy and shown on each puma figure.
The bobcat track is the opposite. Records are abundant, so the work is about distribution: which open-space units bobcats occupy, and which landscape characteristics best explain that pattern.

title: Wild Cats at the Urban Edge
text:
Five questions
The analysis is organised around five pre-registered questions. Each belongs to one track, except the last, which cuts across both:

Landscape. How is protected open space distributed across the ten counties, and how connected or fragmented is it from the view of a wide-ranging carnivore?
Bobcat. Where are bobcats present across open-space units, and which landscape characteristics best explain that pattern?
Puma. Where are the likely movement corridors between core habitat patches, and where do those corridors cross major roads and high-traffic barriers?
Both. Where do the modelled puma corridors cross major roads and high-traffic barriers, and where is wildlife–vehicle collision risk therefore concentrated? Direct mortality records are pending; the road crossings serve as the interim risk proxy.
Cross-cutting. How much of the apparent spatial pattern reflects true distribution, and how much reflects observer and detection effort?

The fifth question is treated as a first-class result, not a footnote. Detection effort shapes every descriptive layer in the project, and the two species answer it in opposite ways: the bobcat model corrects for effort, while the puma corridors do not depend on it. That contrast runs through the sections that follow.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why
text: Bobcats are the easy species to study here, and that ease is itself the problem. Records are abundant, so the question is not whether there is enough data — it is how much of the apparent pattern is bobcats and how much is people with cameras and phones. The occupancy model is built to separate the two.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why
text:
Occupancy, not just sightings
A raw map of bobcat sightings shows where people looked as much as where bobcats are. An occupancy model pulls those apart. It treats each open-space unit as a site visited repeatedly, models the chance of detecting a bobcat given that it is present, and from that estimates the chance the unit is occupied at all. The detection part absorbs the effort; the occupancy part is what’s left.
The fit is a single-species occupancy model over 845 open-space units, built in a fixed two-stage order: the detection sub-model first, then occupancy with the detection structure held fixed. The covariate sets and the selection rule were written down before any fitted number was looked at (Decision 31), so the result is a test of a pre-registered model, not a search for one that fit.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why
text:
Detection is effort, plainly
The detection result is blunt. The single covariate is a per-visit record-count effort proxy, and it dominates: more recording effort, far higher detection, with a strength that leaves no room for doubt. Against a no-effort null the effort model is better by an AICc gap of 408 — not a subtle correction, the main signal in the detection process.
This is the whole reason the occupancy model exists. A sightings map would read that effort as bobcat distribution. The model reads it as effort and sets it aside, so the occupancy surface underneath is not just a map of where people were looking.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why
text:
What explains occupancy
With effort handled, three landscape signals shape where bobcats are. The pattern needs all three parts together — terrain, land cover, and human footprint. The model that keeps only one of them falls far behind: a human-footprint-only or a land-cover-only model sits more than 40 AICc units below the full model, while the full model and its near-twin carry 85% of the weight between them.








Figure 1: Bobcat occupancy coefficients (logit scale, top model m_full), with 95% confidence intervals. Points right of the zero line raise the modelled chance a unit is occupied; points left lower it. Elevation is the strongest signal (positive); human modification (gHM) is the clearest negative. Tree cover leans positive but its interval touches zero. Terrain aspect, slope, grass, and housing density do not separate from zero. Source: Decision 31 occupancy fit (tbl_13).





Elevation is the strongest signal, and it is positive. Bobcat occupancy rises with mean unit elevation — the higher, less-developed units of the Coast Ranges and Diablo are the strongholds. Human modification is the clearest negative. As the gHM index rises, modelled occupancy falls: this is the coexistence limit showing up directly in the numbers. Tree cover leans positive but its interval just touches zero, so it reads as a lean, not a firm effect. Grass cover, slope, terrain aspect, and housing density do not separate from zero in this fit.
The housing result is worth one note. Housing density enters positive but unresolved, while gHM enters clearly negative. The two are correlated, and the project deliberately lets gHM carry the human-pressure axis (Decision 23). Read together, the human signal in bobcat occupancy is real and negative — it just lives in the gHM term, not the housing one.

The occupancy surface
The map below is the model-corrected result: predicted occupancy for each open-space unit, after detection effort has been modelled out. It is the layer to trust for distribution — not the raw sightings, and not the kernel density that follows.








Figure 2: Predicted bobcat occupancy (ψ) by open-space unit, from the model-averaged occupancy fit. Darker green is higher predicted occupancy. Grey units are not modelled — they lack covariate coverage, so no prediction exists; grey means no estimate, not low occupancy. The surface covers the 845 fitted units; the 284 grey units carry geometry only. Detection effort has been modelled out of this surface, which is what separates it from the raw record maps below. Source: model-averaged occu fit (m_full + m_fullgrad).




This surface is where the effort correction pays off. A raw sightings map would put the darkest signal wherever recording is densest — near trailheads, near cities. The occupancy model moves the signal to where the landscape supports bobcats: up in elevation, away from human modification. Where the two disagree is the effort bias made visible, and it is the heart of Question 5.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why
section: Two more views, and why they need care
text:
Two more views, and why they need care
The occupancy surface is the model-corrected view. Two descriptive layers sit alongside it, and both carry the effort problem the occupancy model was built to escape — so both are read with that caveat attached.
Kernel density. A smoothed surface of where bobcat records fall. The smoothing scale — the bandwidth — is set by a pre-registered rule, not by hand and not by the data-driven default, because the default collapses toward a tiny bandwidth that just maps the densest clusters of effort (Decision 28). Even with the rule, a kernel-density surface of opportunistic records maps detection effort as much as bobcat density. It is shown as a descriptive layer, not as an abundance estimate.








Figure 3: Kernel-density surface of bobcat records (500 m, precise records only). Darker green is higher record density. The colour follows a square-root stretch, not a linear one: density is heavily right-skewed, so a linear scale would show only a few peak cells and wash out the rest — the stretch makes the pattern visible but visually lifts the low values, so read colour as relative pattern, not absolute density. Masked and out-of-study cells are transparent, not zero. This surface maps recording effort as much as bobcat density; the occupancy surface above is the layer to trust for distribution. Source: spatstat KDE, bandwidth by Decision 28.




Hot spots. A Getis-Ord Gi* analysis flags units with significantly high or low record counts relative to their neighbours. The honest problem, carried over from the tiger project: a raw-count hot spot is partly an observer-effort hot spot. So each hot unit is cross-read against the effort surface and labelled — TRUSTED where the cluster is not explained by effort, EFFORT-FLAGGED where it is. The map shows the label, not just the count.
The result here is mostly an absence, and that absence is the finding. After false-discovery-rate correction, only six units are significant hot spots out of more than eleven hundred, against 224 significant cold spots. Bobcat records barely cluster into strong hotspots at all once the multiple-testing correction is applied. And of the six hot units, the effort cross-read trusts only four — the other two coincide with recording-effort hotspots and are flagged as suspect. So the honest hot-spot story is: weak positive clustering, two of the few hot units probably an artefact of where people looked, and a much clearer signal in the cold spots — the quiet units where bobcats are recorded less than their surroundings would predict.








Figure 4: Getis-Ord Gi* hot- and cold-spot units for bobcat records, FDR-corrected. Red units are significant hotspots, purple units significant cold spots, faint grey not significant. Solid red is a TRUSTED hotspot; hollow red is a hotspot that coincides with a recording-effort hotspot and is flagged as effort-SUSPECT. Only six units are hot (four trusted, two suspect) against 224 cold — the weakness of the clustering is itself the result, and every count behind it reflects recording effort as much as bobcat presence. Source: sfdep Gi* with the Q5 effort cross-read.

title: Where Bobcats Are, and Why
section: The detection-bias caveat, stated once and carried
text:
The detection-bias caveat, stated once and carried
Every descriptive map in this section — kernel density, hot spots, even the raw record counts behind them — reflects where people recorded bobcats, not only where bobcats are. That is not a footnote to bury; it is the point of Question 5, and it is why the occupancy surface, which models effort explicitly, is the layer to trust for distribution. The two other layers are shown because they are informative about pattern, with the effort caveat attached to each, not because they are unbiased.
This is also the cleanest contrast in the whole project. The bobcat occupancy model corrects for effort and, where it does, its picture diverges from the raw kernel density. The puma corridors in the next section do not depend on effort at all — they are built from landscape resistance, not from sightings — so they converge with the density surface for a different reason. Same region, two species, two entirely different relationships between what was recorded and what is there.

title: What was recorded, and what is there
text:
Every map on this site is built from records that people made. People do not look everywhere equally. They look near roads, near trails, near cities, and in the months of survey drives and community bio-blitzes. So a map of where the records are is partly a map of where the observers were. This is the effort problem, and Q5 asks it directly: how much of the pattern is the animal, and how much is the observer?
This page does not add a new dataset. It reads the puma and the bobcat results against each other, because the two species answer the effort question in opposite ways — and the contrast is itself the finding.






NoteRead this after the Bobcat and Puma pages



Q5 is a cross-read. It uses the bobcat occupancy result (the Bobcat page) and the puma corridor result (the Puma page). If you have not seen those, the short version is below each heading.

title: What was recorded, and what is there
text:
Two species, two relationships
A descriptive surface — a kernel-density map of records, or a hot-spot map — carries the effort signal directly, because it is built from the raw records. The two analytical tracks then do different things with that signal.

Bobcat — the model pulls away from effort. The occupancy model has a separate detection sub-model. It estimates effort and presence as two things, then reports presence with the effort taken out. So the modelled result is expected to move away from the raw record density.
Puma — the model never sees effort at all. The corridor is built from the landscape: land cover, human modification, slope, and traffic (see the Methods page and Decision 26). There is no record-density term anywhere in it. So if the corridor lands on the observed record density, that agreement was not put there by construction.

The result is a divergence for one species and a convergence for the other, and both are honest for the same reason.

Bobcat: modelled occupancy DIVERGES from the record density
The bobcat occupancy surface and the raw kernel-density surface do not match. The correlation between the two is near zero (r = 0.075).
That is the correct outcome, not a failure. The raw density is effort-shaped — high where people surveyed. The occupancy model corrects for that, because its detection sub-model absorbs the survey effort and reports the presence pattern underneath. The two surfaces disagree because the model is doing its job. A high agreement here would have been a warning sign that the model had simply re-drawn the effort map.


Puma: modelled corridor CONVERGES with the record density
The puma corridor is the opposite case, and it also reverses what we expected before we ran it.
The pre-analysis guess was divergence — that the corridor, and especially the Coyote Valley pinch, would thread through low-record gaps, pumas slipping through a developed squeeze unseen. The data says the opposite:

The corridor runs through above-median record density along its whole length. The least-cost path sits at the 77th percentile of the density surface (median across the route), and none of it falls below the median.
The Coyote Valley pinch is at the 83rd percentile — high record density, not the predicted low.
Of the record hot-spots the corridor crosses, six of seven are effort-checked as trusted — real record concentration, not survey artifact.

Two methods that share no effort term — a structure-driven least-cost corridor and an effort-shaped record surface — agree on where the corridor is. Because the corridor model never saw the records, that agreement is evidence the puma pattern is real terrain-driven signal, not an effort shadow.

title: What was recorded, and what is there
text:
The convergence, on the map
The surface below is the puma record density (kernel density, published at the 1 km grain the sensitive-data policy requires — see the note at the foot of this page). On top of it are the two-tier corridor swath and the core habitat patches. Read it for one thing: the corridor band sits on the warmer parts of the surface, not the gaps.








Figure 1: Puma record density (kernel-density surface, 1 km) with the two-tier movement corridor and core habitat patches. The corridor band runs through above-median density along its length, including at the Coyote Valley pinch. Density is a smoothed record surface and is effort-shaped; it is read here only as a cross-check on the structure-built corridor, never as a distribution result on its own.




The density surface is smoothed with a wide (5 km) bandwidth, set from a puma home-range prior. That width is why the map shows broad warm zones, not sharp points — and it is one reason the percentile figures stay in the text and not on the legend: a smoothed surface cannot honestly show a single-cell pinch value.

title: What was recorded, and what is there
section: The record hot-spots, and how many are just effort
text:
The record hot-spots, and how many are just effort
The density surface above is smooth. A hot-spot map is sharper: it marks the open-space units where puma records cluster more than their neighbours, tested for significance. But a record hot-spot has two possible causes — real puma presence, or a place people surveyed hard. The Q5 effort check separates them:

Trusted — the unit is a record hot-spot and not an effort hot-spot. Real concentration.
Suspect — the unit is a record hot-spot and also an effort hot-spot. It may just be where people looked.

The map below draws trusted units as solid fill and suspect units as hollow, dashed outlines. Read the split, not just the count: for puma, about half of all hot units are effort-suspect — far more than for bobcat. That is the effort problem made visible on a single map.








Figure 2: Getis-Ord Gi* hot-spot units for puma records, FDR-corrected. Solid red is a TRUSTED hotspot (record clustering not explained by effort); hollow dashed red is a hotspot that also coincides with a recording-effort hotspot, flagged effort-SUSPECT. About half of all puma hot units are effort-suspect — far more than bobcat — which is the effort problem made visible. Hot-spots are record-driven and effort-shaped; they are not a puma distribution. Source: sfdep Gi* with the Q5 effort cross-read.






Of the puma hot units, the effort cross-read trusts fewer than half; the rest coincide with recording-effort hotspots and are flagged suspect. Any hot unit resting on fewer than three precise records is drawn without a hover label, so a location cannot be narrowed from it (sensitive-data policy §3).
The hot-spot map and the corridor tell the same story from two directions. Where the corridor crosses record hot-spots, most of those units are trusted — real presence, not effort. That is the part of the convergence that is not circular. But across the whole region, the large share of suspect units is the reminder Q5 exists to give: a red unit is not proof of pumas until the effort check clears it.

title: What was recorded, and what is there
section: What this convergence is, and what it is not
text:
What this convergence is, and what it is not
The agreement is real, but it must be read at its true strength — corroboration, not proof.

It is corroboration. Two methods with no shared effort term land in the same places, and most of the record hot-spots on the corridor are effort-checked as trusted. The puma pattern behaves like real terrain-driven signal.
It is only weak-to-moderate, and partly structural. The resistance surface and the density surface share a land-cover and human-modification foundation. So part of the agreement is two views of the same landscape gradient, not two independent confirmations. A corridor built to follow good habitat, checked against records that also concentrate in good habitat, is expected to agree — the ecology literature says as much.
It is not validation. Strong, independent validation needs movement data — GPS collars showing pumas actually using the route. This project has occurrence records only. The corridor is a plausible, record-corroborated hypothesis, not a confirmed path.

Two things keep the convergence meaningful in spite of the shared foundation. The trusted hot-spots are record concentration that is not effort-driven — real presence on the corridor. And the corridor carries a road-and-traffic term the density surface does not have — so the two are not the same construct, and agreement across that difference is more than shared-terrain overlap.






ImportantWhy we lead with the band, not the line



The corridor is shown as a two-tier swath, not a single line. Against simulated true movement, the precise least-cost centre-line is the least accurate connectivity form, while a swath overlaps true movement far better. The line is a tidy artifact of the algorithm; the band is the more honest product. This is why the pinch percentile (83rd) is the cell value near the route, not an on-line reading — at 1 km grain the centre-line passes about 1.6 km from the exact pinch cell.

title: What was recorded, and what is there
text:
The shared caveat, stated once
Both species inherit the same ceiling, and it is the point of Q5: descriptive record surfaces are effort-shaped. A kernel-density map or a raw hot-spot map shows where records concentrate, and records concentrate where people looked. The two tracks handle this differently — the bobcat occupancy model removes the effort signal and so diverges from the raw surface; the puma corridor never contains an effort signal and so its convergence with the raw surface is informative rather than circular — but neither track escapes the fact that the underlying records were made by people, unevenly. Every descriptive map on this site should be read with that in mind.






NoteSensitive-data note (puma)



Precise puma locations are withheld. iNaturalist does not obscure mountain lions in California, so this project holds precise records that could expose real animals if published as points. The density surface on this page is published only at a 1 km grain, which cannot be reversed to a location, and it clears the project’s publish gate at that grain. No puma points, den sites, or kill sites appear anywhere on this site.
